ABSTRACT 25

Introduc/on 26

Drug resistance in Neisseria gonorrhoeae is an urgent public health threat. The an/cipated 27

approval of two new an/microbials for gonorrhea prompts the need for evidence-based rollout 28

strategies that minimize drug resistance. 29

Methods 30

We used a stochas/c compartmental model of men who have sex with men (MSM) in the 31

United States (U.S.) to compare two main strategies—equal alloca/on and sequen/al drug 32

deployment—for two new and one exis/ng drug and measured the /me for each drug to reach 33

a resistance prevalence threshold of 5%. We conducted broad analyses assessing the sensi/vity 34

of our results to wide varia/on in parameters governing the baseline behavior of the model and 35

drug resistance evolu/on and ﬁtness. 36

Results 37

Compared to the equal alloca/on strategy, the sequen/al strategy had reached the resistance 38

prevalence threshold i) for each drug individually in at least as many simula/ons; ii) for all three 39

drugs in at least as many simula/ons; and iii) for at least as many drugs on average. Aber 10 40

years, no equal alloca/on strategy simula/ons had met the 5% resistance prevalence threshold 41

for any of the drugs, whereas 99.6% of sequen/al simula/ons had for the ﬁrst drug, of which 42

3.5% had also met the threshold for the second drug. The sequen/al strategy was worse for 43

nearly every reasonable combina/on of model parameters. 44

Conclusion 45

In a model of U.S. MSM, the equal alloca/on strategy for introducing new drugs for gonorrhea 46

matched or outperformed the strategy of sequen/al introduc/on in terms of resistance 47

prevalence. 48

INTRODUCTION 59

The burden of disease caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae and the emergence of extremely drug- 60

resistant strains highlights the need for evidence to op/mize treatment op/ons. N. gonorrhoeae 61

is an obligate human bacterial pathogen that causes the sexually transmided infec/on (STI) 62

gonorrhea. There were an es/mated 82.4 million gonorrhea infec/ons worldwide in 2020 and 63

over half a million in the United States (U.S.) in 2023.1,2 High-risk demographics in the U.S. 64

include young adults (especially ages 20-24), men who have sex with men (MSM), and those 65

iden/fying as American Indian, Alaskan Na/ve, or Black or African American.2 Gonorrhea 66

treatment guidelines in the U.S. recommend a 500 mg intramuscular injec/on with cebriaxone, 67

but strains resistant to cebriaxone have spread globally.3–8 Unlike other common STI pathogens, 68

N. gonorrhoeae has evolved resistance to every an/bio/c approved to treat it.9 69

Two new ﬁrst-in-class an/bio/cs have recently reported posi/ve phase III trial results for 70

gonorrhea treatment: zoliﬂodacin and gepo/dacin.10,11 Zoliﬂodacin is a single-dose oral 71

regimen, while the gepo/dacin regimen in the phase III study was two oral doses taken 10-12 72

hours apart. Upon their approval for gonorrhea treatment, recommenda/ons will be required 73

to guide clinical prac/ce. 74

Modeling studies have examined similar ques/ons about how best to roll out interven/ons for 75

gonorrhea.12–14 Most relatedly, one study assessed mul/ple strategies for introducing one new 76

an/bio/c for gonorrhea using a determinis/c modeling framework.12 It found that keeping the 77

new drug in reserve un/l the currently used therapy reached its resistance prevalence threshold 78

was consistently worse than strategies that deployed the new drug upon approval. Other 79

studies have assessed interven/ons including point-of-care tes/ng, rapid suscep/bility tes/ng, 80

15–18 vaccina/on,13,14,19 screening,  and post-exposure prophylaxis.20–22 No study so far has 81

considered the availability of two new drug op/ons for the treatment of gonorrhea and used a 82

stochas/c framework aimed at capturing stochas/c resistance emergence and ex/nc/on 83

dynamics. 84

In this study, we compared rollout strategies for two new treatment op/ons in addi/on to one 85

exis/ng therapy using a stochas/c compartmental model of gonorrhea in U.S. MSM. We 86

assessed which rollout strategy maximized the useful lifespan of the three poten/al treatment 87

op/ons and which combina/ons of parameters most inﬂuenced this result. 88

METHODS 90

Model Structure and Implementa7on 91

We used a compartmental model of gonorrhea transmission among U.S. MSM adapted from 92

previous studies.12,15,16,20 Brieﬂy, the model follows suscep/ble-infected-suscep/ble (SIS) 93

dynamics. Treatment is successful unless there is resistance to the drug used, in which case 94

treatment fails. We modeled three general drugs, A, B, and C, to represent cebriaxone, 95

zoliﬂodacin, and gepo/dacin, respec/vely, acknowledging that the precise parameters (e.g., 96

likelihood of emergence of resistance and ﬁtness cost) for these speciﬁc drugs remain unknown. 97

The popula/on is stra/ﬁed into high-, medium-, and low-risk, which describe the number of 98

partnerships formed by individuals in each stratum. Mixing is not fully assorta/ve; partnerships 99

can be formed within one’s own risk stratum and outside of it. All compartments and transi/ons 100

between them are shown in Supplementary Figure 1 and described in Appendix I & II. 101

There are two sets of infected compartments: symptoma/c (Y) and asymptoma/c (Z). 102

Symptoma/c individuals are assumed to seek treatment, whereas asymptoma/c individuals are 103

only detected and treated at the rate of asymptoma/c screening. There is an addi/onal exit rate 104

from symptoma/c compartments represen/ng the possibility of seeking care for retreatment if 105

symptoms do not resolve aber failing treatment. Resistance can occur through two mechanisms 106

in the model: 1) star/ng resistance is transmided, meaning that previously uninfected 107

individuals are directly infected with resistant bacteria, or 2) people infected with strains that 108

are suscep/ble to the an/bio/c with which they are treated develop resistance to that 109

an/bio/c. Resistance can only arise to one an/bio/c at a /me, as infected individuals are 110

treated with a single an/bio/c, though mul/-drug resistance can emerge on already resistant 111

backgrounds. 112

Transmission, care seeking, screening, natural recovery, and resistance emergence were 113

modeled as a con/nuous /me Markov chain with event rates (Appendix II) matching those of 114

the determinis/c system (Appendix I). The system was then simulated in discrete /me using 115

binomial 𝜏-leaping with a /me step of one day.23,24 The implementa/on of this approach 116

involved mul/nomial draws from each compartment at each /me step. This stochas/c 117

framework captures rare resistance emergence events and lineage ex/nc/ons, which govern 118

diﬀerences in dynamics between diﬀerent rollout strategies.25 119

The models were implemented in R 4.4.1 using the Odin package26 and run on the FASRC 120

Cannon high performance compu/ng cluster at Harvard University. All code used in this project 121

can be found at: hdps://github.com/gradlab/MK_twodrugintro_public. 122

123

Strategy Comparison 124

We compared two drug rollout strategies: sequen/al and equal alloca/on. In each strategy, 125

individuals are treated with one drug at a /me. At the beginning of the sequen/al strategy, 126

everyone is treated with drug A. Once the resistance prevalence threshold is met for drug A, it 127

phases out and is replaced by B. Once the resistance prevalence threshold is met for drug B, it 128

phases out and is replaced by C un/l the end of the simula/on. At the beginning of the equal 129

alloca/on strategy, each infected individual has a 1/3 chance of being treated with drug A, drug 130

B, or drug C. Once the ﬁrst drug hits its resistance prevalence threshold, it is no longer used; 131

treatment is then either of the two remaining drugs, each with a 1/2 chance. When the 132

resistance prevalence threshold is met for the second drug, it phases out. The third drug is then 133

used for the rest of the simula/on (Supplementary Figure 2). 134

In both strategies, people with symptoma/c infec/ons have a chance to seek retreatment, in 135

which case they are treated with a last resort treatment that is not drugs A, B, or C, such as 136

ertapenem.5 Retreatment is assumed to always be successful. We did not explore combina/on 137

Parameter Selec7on and Sensi7vity Analysis 144

Model parameters were selected by literature search, maximum likelihood es/ma/on 145

calibra/on, and sensi/vity analysis (Supplementary Table 1, Supplementary Table 2). 146

Parameters were divided into two categories: those governing underlying transmission 147

dynamics (Group 1), and those rela/ng to drug resistance emergence and persistence (Group 2). 148

For Group 1 parameters, which were unlikely to aﬀect strategy ordering, we iden/ﬁed star/ng 149

values from the literature and calibrated a drug A-only model run for two years using the R 150

bbmle package as described.12,29 We then conducted a La/n hypercube sampling (LHS) 151

sensi/vity analysis over all possible values of the calibrated parameters to increase our 152

conﬁdence in the calibrated parameter values. 153

We did not calibrate Group 2 parameters and instead performed a broad LHS sensi/vity analysis 154

(Supplementary Table 2). These parameters included the probability of resistance emerging on 155

treatment, the rela/ve transmissibility cost (rela/ve ﬁtness) of drug resistance, and the star/ng 156

number of cases of resistance in the system.  While these quan//es are diﬃcult to ascertain 157

empirically, we can roughly bound the probability of resistance emerging on treatment using 158

the subs/tu/on rate and observed treatment failures. The N. gonorrhoeae subs/tu/on rate is 159

on the order of 10-6 subs/tu/ons per site per year in magnitude.30 This is the rate of neutral 160

muta/ons that have established, and therefore a lower bound on the order of magnitude for 161

our model’s muta/on probability parameter as muta/ons that are selected are more likely to 162

establish.  While the upper bound is more challenging, a muta/on probability of 10-4 or above 163

would mean that there were more than one treatment failures per 10000 cases, which would 164

amount to at least 60 treatment failures in the US in 2023. To be conserva/ve, we explored 165

muta/on probabili/es one order of magnitude outside of what we thought most likely (10-3 - 10- 166

7). 167

We used LHS (the lhs package in R31,32) for both sensi/vity analyses to eﬃciently and 168

comprehensively survey a mul/dimensional parameter space. For each sensi/vity analysis, we 169

generated 1000 unique sets of parameter combina/ons. For each parameter combina/on, we 170

ran 100 stochas/c simula/ons of each strategy. 171

Models run with the baseline parameter set showed that the equal alloca/on strategy was 175

consistently beder than the sequen/al strategy (Figure 1). At each /me step, the same number 176

or fewer simula/ons had met the 5% resistance prevalence threshold to each of the three drugs 177

under the equal alloca/on strategy compared to the sequen/al strategy. By year ﬁve, no equal 178

99.6% of sequen/al strategy simula/ons had reached 5% resistance prevalence for drug A, and 182

30 years, 25.2% of equal alloca/on strategy whereas 100% of sequen/al strategy simula/ons 184

At every /me point, the sequen/al strategy had lost at least as many of the three available 188

3 drugs, Supplementary Figure 3). 197

Similarly, across the study dura/on, the sequen/al strategy had lost all three drugs in the same 198

The equal alloca/on strategy also outperformed the sequen/al strategy at resistance 203

DISCUSSION 227

In our modeling study, the equal alloca/on strategy, in which the two new an/bio/cs and the 228

currently used therapy are deployed in equal propor/on, randomly across the popula/on 229

treated, minimized the emergence and spread of an/bio/c resistance when compared to a 230

strategy of rolling out the new drugs sequen/ally. Under the baseline set of parameters, 231

resistance to all three treatments was less likely to reach a 5% prevalence threshold in the equal 232

alloca/on strategy than in the sequen/al strategy. This result held at resistance prevalence 233

thresholds for drug loss of 1% and 10%. Across the simula/on period, more drugs on average 234

were lost due to an/microbial resistance under the sequen/al strategy than under the equal 235

alloca/on strategy. Our results were robust to a wide range of parameters that alter gonorrhea 236

transmission dynamics. 237

The model results were most sensi/ve to the number of cases of star/ng resistance, the 238

probability of resistance emergence, and the rela/ve ﬁtness. Our sensi/vity analysis showed 239

that it was possible to derive parameter combina/ons where the equal alloca/on strategy 240

performed worse than the sequen/al strategy, but this required extreme and unlikely 241

combina/ons of parameter values. Of the 22 parameter combina/ons where the equal 242

alloca/on strategy had lost, on average, more drugs than the sequen/al strategy by year 10, 243

only a small propor/on of simula/ons had lost any drugs under equal alloca/on; a maximum 6% 244

of simula/ons had met the 5% prevalence threshold for drug B or drug C. In these scenarios, 245

drug A never reached its resistance prevalence threshold and therefore drugs B and C were 246

never used in the sequen/al strategy; in contrast, their use in the equal alloca/on strategy 247

meant that in some scenarios emerging or preexis/ng resistance to these drugs propagated and 248

reached the threshold. 249

We classiﬁed the majority of the 22 parameter combina/ons where equal alloca/on was worse 250

into “Class I”, where at least one emergence probability was greater than 10-4 (Supplementary 251

*Figure 6). For example, in one parameter combina/on, the probability of resistance emerging 252*

on treatment with drug B was 2.86 x 10-4, which would mean that, for 600,000 cases of 253

gonorrhea treated with drug B, about 200 would fail treatment, which is an improbably high 254

probability for drug A such that the resistance prevalence threshold for drug A was never met 260

and therefore drugs B and C were never used under the sequen/al strategy (Supplementary 261

*Table 4, Supplementary Figure 7). Even when this occurred, only 1-2% of simula/ons had 262*

reached the resistance prevalence threshold for drugs B or C aber 10 years under the equal 263

alloca/on strategy. This emphasizes that the cases where the sequen/al strategy outperformed 264

the equal alloca/on strategy were edge cases involving a co-occurrence of unlikely events. 265

Several factors not considered in this study may impact rollout decisions. Here, we focused on 266

an MSM-only sexual network in the U.S., thus these results may not generalize to other sexual 267

network structures or country senngs with higher baseline cebriaxone resistance prevalences 268

and diﬀerent asymptoma/c screening prac/ces. Considera/ons of drug price, availability, 269

preferences for modes of administra/on, and toxici/es were not included but will be important 270

drivers of drug use and resistance paderns that will also depend on context. 271

We modeled a closed system with no importa/on of drug resistance and did not include the 272

eﬀects of bystander selec/on for drug resistance due to an/bio/c use for indica/ons outside of 273

gonorrhea. We assumed that all drug resistance caused treatment failure and did not model 274

within-individual evolu/on and varia/on that may occur along a transmission chain. We ﬁxed 275

parameter values in each simula/on, so that, for example, the rela/ve ﬁtness of a par/cular 276

padern of resistance did not change over /me. Our probability of resistance emergence on 277

treatment broadly referred to any kind of gene/c event leading to resistance but did not 278

diﬀeren/ate between point muta/ons or recombina/on events, which could vary by drug and 279

have diﬀerent rates. There is also substan/al uncertainty surrounding the parameter values 280

governing our models. However, we note that our results held across nearly all possible 281

combina/ons of the parameter values and form a baseline intui/on about drug resistance 282

dynamics to be expanded upon in the future. 283

Our framework can be used for further inves/ga/ons, including evalua/ng strategies where all 284

drugs are available, but some are used more than others, the impact of drug synergy and cross 285

resistance, given that zoliﬂodacin and gepo/dacin target the same molecular complex as 286

ﬂuoroquinolones, and adap/ve strategies that change in response to data on the likelihood of 287

emergence of resistance and the rela/ve ﬁtness cost of resistance. Alterna/ve screening 288

strategies could also meaningfully impact resistance minimiza/on; future studies building on 289

our work could explore expedited partner therapy, rapid gonorrhea tests and rapid 290

suscep/bility tes/ng, and vaccine usage. 291

In conclusion, introducing two new an/microbials to treat gonorrhea alongside the currently 292

used treatment was more eﬀec/ve at minimizing drug resistance than introducing the drugs in 293

sequence. Our results reinforce that distribu/ng the selec/ve pressures across the popula/on 294

minimizes the emergence of drug resistance (Supplementary Figure 8). This aligns with 295

determinis/c modeling evalua/ng the introduc/on of one new treatment for gonorrhea, and 296
